question: A model reads "She finished her sales pitch and waited" in one conversation and "After a week of rain, the muddy pitch was unplayable" in another, and handles "pitch" correctly both times. Which idea from the lecture explains this?

options.text: The model has two separate tokens, one for each of the two meanings of "pitch"
options.feedback: A token is just a number for a string of characters, so both sentences hand the model the same token. The difference arises afterwards, when the embedding is moved by context.

options.text: The MLP (multi-layer perceptron) stores a definition for each meaning and selects one
options.feedback: The MLP holds no definitions and does no selecting; it is weight matrices that nudge an embedding along. The sentence-by-sentence difference comes from attention, which reads the surrounding words.

options.text: Attention lets the surrounding words move "pitch" to a different place in each sentence
options.feedback: Attention averages in the tokens that came before, so "sales" pulls the embedding toward persuasion while "rain" and "muddy" pull it toward a playing field. Same starting embedding, different weighted average, different meaning.

options.text: The model memorized both sentences during training
options.feedback: Training teaches the model to guess the next word, not to store sentences. Even for a sentence it has never seen, attention can use the words present to settle what "pitch" means.
